# Copy-on-Write Memory in Operating Systems

Copy-on-write (COW) is a memory management optimization in which multiple processes (or multiple mappings within one process) initially share the same physical pages, marked read-only. When any party attempts to write to a shared page, the hardware raises a protection fault; the kernel then transparently allocates a private copy of that page for the writer, updates its page tables, and resumes execution. The result is that memory is duplicated lazily—only for pages that are actually modified—rather than eagerly at the moment sharing is established.

# How Database Indexes Affect Range Queries and Writes

Database indexes are auxiliary data structures that let the engine locate rows without scanning an entire table. The most common index is a B-tree (or B+tree), which keeps keys in sorted order and supports both equality lookups and range scans in O(log n) time. This article explains how indexes change the cost of range queries and writes, with worked examples and a discussion of the limitations that make indexing a trade-off rather than a free lunch.

# Handling Clock Skew in Distributed Systems

## Introduction

A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that communicate over a network and appear to users as a single coherent system. One of the most subtle and persistent challenges in such systems is **clock skew**: the phenomenon where physical clocks on different machines disagree about the current time.
